sentences.text: Carnotaurus was a lightly built, bipedal predator that measured between 7.5 and 8 meters in length and weighed between 1.3 and 2.1 metric tons.
At 7.5 to 8 meters long, the known individual of Carnotaurus represents one of the largest abelisaurids.
Carnotaurus had a skull measuring 59.6 cm in length that was proportionally shorter and deeper than any other large carnivorous dinosaur.
Carnotaurus had a neck that was nearly straight and unusually wide, especially at its base, unlike the S-curve seen in other theropods.
Carnotaurus's forearm was only one-quarter the size of its upper arm.
Carnotaurus is the first known theropod dinosaur to have a significant number of fossil skin impressions found on its skeleton.
The skin of Carnotaurus consisted of a mosaic of polygonal, non-overlapping scales that were approximately 5 to 12 millimeters in diameter.
Carnotaurus was highly adapted for running and was possibly one of the fastest large theropods, reaching speeds of approximately 56 km/h.
Carnotaurus had a safety factor of 92, suggesting its skull was over-engineered compared to the forces generated by its bite.
The holotype skeleton of Carnotaurus was discovered in 1984 in the Chubut Province of Argentina within the La Colonia Formation.
The only known skeleton of Carnotaurus was unearthed in 1984 by an expedition led by paleontologist José Bonaparte.
José Bonaparte named the genus and species Carnotaurus sastrei in 1985 based on a brief description of the skull and lower jaw.
The species name "sastrei" honors Anselmo Sastre, the owner of the estancia where the first and only specimen was found in Chubut, Argentina.
Researchers suggest the distinctive horns and muscular neck of Carnotaurus may have been used in intraspecific fighting.
Studies propose that rivaling Carnotaurus individuals may have fought using quick head blows, slow skull pushes, or head-on ramming with horns acting as shock absorbers.
In 1998, researchers suggested Carnotaurus used its horns for ramming, calculating its neck muscles could withstand collisions at speeds of 5.7 meters per second.
Fernando Novas suggested in 2009 that Carnotaurus's short skull and muscular neck were adaptations for delivering quick, strong head blows.
While Carnotaurus's diet is not fully clear, some studies of its skull morphology suggest it was capable of hunting large prey like sauropods.
A 2009 study estimated the bite force of Carnotaurus at approximately 3,341 newtons.
A 2022 study estimated the anterior bite force of Carnotaurus at around 3,392 newtons, slightly higher than a previous estimate.
Analysis by Mazzetta et al. suggests Carnotaurus was capable of rapid but not strong bites.
Calculations suggest the caudofemoralis muscle in Carnotaurus had a mass of 111 to 137 kg per leg.
Carnotaurus likely had diminished ability to make tight turns because its stiff tail and hip had to move simultaneously.
CT scans revealed the endocranial cavity of Carnotaurus had a volume of 168.8 cm³.
Studies published in 2021 suggest that the larger feature scales on Carnotaurus were randomly distributed along the body rather than arranged in discrete rows as previously depicted.
Researchers suggest that the variation in scale size on Carnotaurus may have helped regulate body heat through thermoregulation.
Carnotaurus is a derived member of the Abelisauridae family, a group of large theropods that dominated predatory niches in southern Gondwana during the late Cretaceous.
Carnotaurus is a well-understood genus within the family Abelisauridae, which was restricted to the southern supercontinent Gondwana.
Carnotaurus belongs to the parent group Furileusauria.
Carnotaurus lived in South America during the Late Cretaceous period, approximately 69 to 66 million years ago.
Carnotaurus fossils date to the Maastrichtian to lower Danian ages, approximately 69 to 64 million years ago.
Carnotaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 72 to 69.9 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage, in what is now South America.
In 2020, Cerroni and colleagues agreed the horns supported keratinous sheaths but argued these sheaths were not much longer than the bony cores.
The function of Carnotaurus's horns is debated, with theories ranging from fighting conspecifics or killing prey to display for courtship or species recognition.
François Therrien and colleagues (2005) questioned earlier interpretations, suggesting Carnotaurus had a bite force twice that of the American alligator.
